theme: Remember your Creator; fear God and keep his commandments
readingInstruction: Read Ecclesiastes 11:1-12:14. The Preacher’s final words call the young to remember their Creator, describe old age, and give the conclusion of the whole book. Read the last two verses slowly.
settingTheScene: The book comes to its end. After exploring the vanity of life under the sun, the Preacher now speaks to the young, then to the old, and then gives his closing verdict. An unnamed editor adds a few words about the Preacher. The conclusion is the key to the entire book and answers the question “What is the point?”
observation: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days” (11:1).
“As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything” (11:5).
“Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth… But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment” (11:9).
“Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come” (12:1).
The poem of old age: the keepers of the house tremble, the grinders cease, the almond tree blossoms, the silver cord is snapped (12:3-6).
“And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (12:7).
“The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd” (12:11).

“The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil” (12:13-14).
interpretation:
Chapter 11 is an encouragement to generosity and bold action. “Cast your bread upon the waters.” Take risks in giving and investing, because you cannot know what will come. The one who waits for perfect conditions never sows or reaps. We cannot know the work of God, so we should act in faith and diligence. “In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand.”

The Preacher then speaks to the young. “Rejoice in your youth.” He does not tell the young to be glum. But he adds a sobering note: God will bring you into judgment. Joy and accountability go together. And in chapter 12, he gives the command: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.” Do it before it is too late, before the “evil days” of old age come.

The poem on old age is one of the most moving in the Bible. It describes a house falling apart: the trembling of the arms, the stooping of the legs, the loss of teeth, dimming eyes, deafness, fear of heights, white hair, and finally death, when “the silver cord is snapped.” It is a vivid portrait of how bodies fail. Its purpose is not morbid but sobering: remember your Creator now.

The last words give the book’s conclusion: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.” After exploring everything under the sun, the Preacher returns to the theme that began Proverbs. The answer to vanity is not found in more experience but in the fear of God. And life matters because “God will bring every deed into judgment.” Nothing is meaningless, because everything will be seen and weighed by him.

Verse 11 says that the words of the wise are like goads and nails, given by “one Shepherd.” The book of Ecclesiastes, with its challenging honesty, is part of God’s shepherding word. It pushes us toward what matters.
connection: Paul says, “The fear of the Lord” and judgment are intertwined: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). Jesus is the “one Shepherd” (John 10:11, 16), the Good Shepherd who gives us the words of life. “Remember your Creator” echoes Mark 10:14-15 and 2 Timothy 3:15. The “whole duty of man” is fulfilled in Christ, who kept the commandments perfectly, and in whom we are forgiven (Romans 8:3-4).
application:
Do something generous without waiting for the perfect time.

If you are young, remember your Creator now. If you are older, tell someone younger what you have learned.

Write down the Preacher’s conclusion, and ask what it means for how you spend this week.
prayerPrompts: Remember your Creator in your own words, and thank him for something from your youth or now.
Ask him to teach you to fear him and keep his commandments.
